processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by melting raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %) in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
Ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Homogenized ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching.
Solution-treated samples were aged at temperatures between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, followed by water quenching. For this sample the aging condition is 650 °C for 6 h.

structures.overall_structure: After aging the 19Al alloy at 650 °C for 6 h, the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn; a great amount of new BCC phase was observed within the β-Mn. The EBSD phase map for this condition is uniform green (β-Mn) with dispersed fine particles.
structures.microstructure_counts: Volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates = 6.5% (19Al aged at 650 °C for 6 h).

phases_present.morphology: dominant near-equiaxed matrix phase; phase map essentially uniform green β-Mn
fine dispersed particles within the β-Mn
fine particles at the β-Mn interfaces

interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. For the 19Al alloy the α→β-Mn transformation required 10 h at 550 °C and was complete after only 1 h at 600 °C and above.
interfaces.interface_notes: New BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the interfaces between the β-Mn; the BCC phase is attributed to enrichment of the BCC-stabilizing element Al around the β-Mn interfaces, while the FCC Cu-rich phase forms due to the limited solubility of Cu. The content of the FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreased with increasing Al content (lowest for 19Al).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and averaged.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: Hardening effect / achievable Vickers hardness after aging

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times, values given by the average of 5 measurements
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the aged samples after different aging treatments
characterization_methods.key_findings: 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 6 h: 810.9 ± 21.7 HV (Table 4).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM; scanning step size 1.5 μm for low magnification and 0.05 μm for high magnification
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: EBSD of the electrolytically polished 19Al sample aged at 650 °C for 6 h; phase maps with legend BCC, α-Mn, β-Mn, FCC
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the constituent phases and the α→β-Mn transformation after aging
characterization_methods.key_findings: For 19Al aged at 650 °C for 6 h the phase map is essentially uniform green β-Mn; the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn and a great amount of new BCC phase was observed within the β-Mn; the combined FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitate volume fraction was 6.5%.

unmapped_findings: The 19Al alloy (Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0 at.% by EDS; density 6.66 g/cm³) aged at 650 °C for 6 h is the exact condition used in EBSD Fig. 6(c) where the phase map is uniform green β-Mn with dispersed fine red particles annotated 'New BCC phase'.

Although this sample (19Al, 650 °C/6 h) has a Vickers hardness of 810.9 HV, the peak hardness of the 19Al alloy (917.8 HV) was achieved at 600 °C for 10 h — a different aging condition, and the fracture-toughness (3.5 MPa·m^1/2) and nanoindentation measurements were made on that hardest state, not on the 650 °C/6 h sample.

For the 19Al alloy, the α→β-Mn transformation needed 10 h at 550 °C and was complete after only 1 h at 600 °C and above; the optimum aging temperature range for achieving ultra-high hardness was 575–625 °C.

Increasing Al content slowed the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn (attributed to Al enrichment around β-Mn hindering growth, and to the Al-stabilized D0₃ phase) and decreased the ductile FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces, thereby lowering the final hardening effect and fracture toughness.
